4) Although the CLCE material is designed to undergo color changes via strain-induced
pitch variation in its chiral nematic structure, the apparent color tunability and
controllability remain limited compared with the reported CLCEs.
Our response:
We thank the reviewer for this important comment. We acknowledge that the structural
color of SS-CLCE does have limited color contrast compared to many previously reported
CLCEs. Here, we would like to explain that there are multiple factors contributing to the
relatively light (fair) color.
First, the synthesis ratio of LC oligomers has a significant impact on color rendering. In
this work, to prepare oligomers and form a small amount of side chains with remaining
thiol end-capping after polymerization, we adopted an extreme molar ratio of acrylate
groups to thiol groups of 1:0.99. This ratio leads to the continuous progress of the chain
extension addition reaction, tending to form longer linear chains. However, longer linear
chains are not a positive factor for N* phase self-assembly. This factor has been elaborated
in the work of Li et al. (Advanced Functional Materials. 2025, 35, 2413965) When the ratio
of acrylate to thiol is close to 1:1, the structural color will be of medium quality.
Second, the microphase separation strategy we employed also exerts an influence on the
presentation of structural color. As we explained in our response to Suggestion 2, the
oligomer undergoes spontaneous arrangement of long chains before polymerization,
thereby gradually forming large-scale crystalline regions. Although we chose to carry out
the polymerization process before the formation of the crystalline region, the arrangement
process obviously has a negative impact on the uniform vertical alignment of the N*
helical structure.
Third, it is the for choosing the solvent evaporation method. The solvent evaporation
method is a simple approach for preparing LCEs. It enables the vertical alignment of the
helical axes of CLCEs through the orientation force generated by solvent evaporation.
However, due to the long spacing and high viscosity of the LC oligomers, this method can
only achieve limited effectiveness. Nevertheless, it is convenient and feasible, eliminating
the need for LC cell preparation and the corresponding manufacturing processes, as well
as reducing restrictions on molds, thereby facilitating the preparation of large-area thin
films. Additionally, although the strong anchoring effect of the alignment layer in the LC
cell is sufficient to induce nearly perfect alignment of the oligomers, the lack of a swollen
network and the constraints on the movement of polymer chains are unfavorable for the
subsequent occurrence of phase separation.
In summary, there are multiple factors contributing to the limitations of structural color.
However, we still take pride in the goal we have achieved—realizing stiffness switching
of single-layer free-standing chiral liquid crystal elastomer (CLCE) films via a simple
method. Currently, in the CLCE system, there are relatively few references regarding this
target, which indicates greater room for improvement, both in terms of color and the degree
of stiffness enhancement.
As a signature characteristic of CLCEs, their structural color indeed requires
additional attention. On the premise of maintaining the original mechanical
properties, stiffness switching performance, and phase separation strategy
unchanged, we have updated the physical display image (Fig. 5c) to improve the image
quality as much as possible.
To clarify the limitations of structural color, we have revised the manuscript as follows:
"Overall, the color change in the film was uniform, demonstrating its soft-elastic behavior.
It should also be noted that the structural color exhibited by SS-CLCEs has certain
limitations compared with existing CLCEs, which is attributed to the molar ratio of acrylate
to thiol (used for oligomer preparation) being close to 1:1, as well as the selection of the
microphase separation strategy and the solvent evaporation method. The trade-off involved
causes SS-CLCEs to sacrifice the quality of structural color in exchange for switchable
mechanical properties.63" (Highlighted in Results, page 16, lines 316-321)
"63 Li, S. et al. Direct Ink Writing of Cephalopod Skin-Like Core-Shell Fibers From
Cholesteric Liquid Crystal Elastomers and Dyed Solutions. Adv. Funct. Mater. 35,
2413965 (2025). "

5) The statement on Page 19, Lines 359–361: “SS-CLCE can fully soften within 10 seconds
when heated to 80 °C and remain flexible for the following 8 hours, allowing for large and

not discuss what mechanical or structural changes occur if the sample is maintained at

physical crosslinks that enhance stiffness”. Given the importance of thermal programming
and retention in shape memory materials, this point should be further investigated.
Our response:
We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. There may be a misunderstanding
arising from insufficient clarity in our expression. Based on the DSC curves of SS-CLCEs
(Figure R3), we can observe that both the isotropic phase transition temperature of
the smectic phase and the melting range of polymer crystallization are below 80 °C.
Therefore, we selected 80 °C to eliminate these phase separations, thereby achieving
the effect of softening the material. Next, the SS-CLCE was placed at a low
temperature (room temperature) to undergo the spontaneous phase separation for
reinforcement and toughening. Regarding the mentioned 8 hours, this duration was also
selected based on the modulus-time curve during the material's self-reinforcement process
(Figure R4). The S-shaped curve exhibits a slow-fast-slow reinforcement rate. Before 8
hours, the reinforcement rate is slow and the effect is not significant (2.22 MPa to 6.54
MPa); therefore, we state that the material remains soft and highly deformable within 8
hours.
After the SS-CLCE is heated and softened at a high temperature of 80 °C to eliminate phase
separation, it becomes soft; subsequently, under conditions below the crystal melting point

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
This work presents a stiffness-switchable chiral liquid crystal elastomer (SS-CLCE) that
achieves intrinsic 4D memory of both shape and structural color. By introducing long side

stiffens over time, enabling high-fidelity shape and color retention without external energy
input. The system allows full reset via heating, facilitating recyclable and reprogrammable
applications such as rewritable encryption layers. This approach transforms traditional
material aging into a programmable feature, offering a new design paradigm for
multifunctional, energy-efficient smart polymers. In addition, reprogramming via
microphase separation is highly innovative in the field of LCEs. Overall, the paper is well-
organized and written. The topic and the quality match the requirements of Nature
Communications. There are some comments for authors to consider.
Our response:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's positive and encouraging evaluation of this work.
These comments and suggestions have actively helped us improve the quality of the
manuscript. We have addressed all points raised from the reviewer and revised the
manuscript where necessary. Please see our detailed response below.
1) What is the relationship between the smectic, nematic, and chiral phases? In typical
experiments, specific mesogens (such as C6BAPE) are usually required to obtain smectic-
phase LCEs. However, in this work, RM82 alone can induce the smectic phase. What are
the conditions for the transition from a (chiral) nematic phase to a (chiral) smectic phase?
Can the smectic and nematic phases coexist in LCE?
Our response:
We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment. All these three phases result from the
self-assembly of LC molecules into specific arrangements. Generally, with increasing
temperature, LC phases undergo a transition from smectic phase to nematic phase and then
to isotropic phase, realizing an order-to-disorder transformation. This constitutes a
temperature-dependent hierarchy of structural order. Chiral nematic phase is a variant of
the nematic phase, formed by intrinsically chiral LC molecules or achiral LC molecules
doped with chiral agents at an appropriate temperature. This reflects the influence of
chirality on the nematic phase.
We fully agree that specific mesogens play a decisive role in smectic phase formation,
which is a result of the fact that the LC rod-like cores and flexible chains themselves are
adapted to the lamellar arrangement of the smectic phase. Meanwhile, the elastomer
formed by RM82—a commonly used nematic monomer—after undergoing specific
synthesis steps also has the possibility of exhibiting a smectic phase. For instance, in this
work, we used long-chain thiols to undergo an addition reaction with RM82, forming a
linear structure of "long flexible chain–rod-like mesogen–long flexible chain". After
polymerization, the resulting structure exhibits low cross-linking density and high chain
mobility. The self-assembly of mesogenic cores induces core-chain hierarchy, i.e., the
formation of a lamellar structure. Naturally, the influence of this tendency is limited;
moreover, in a multi-domain cross-linked network, it is unable to form the nearly perfect
smectic phase alignment. Furthermore, our research findings are consistent with previous
studies (Ref. 40). Owing to the aforementioned arrangement and the coexistence of main
chains and side chains in the polymer, the transition from the nematic phase to the smectic
phase at an appropriate temperature is incomplete. Therefore, it is possible that the smectic
and nematic phases coexist in LCE. (Advanced Functional Materials, 2023, 33, 2214918.)
2) How is the formation of the smectic phase related to the chemical composition and
network structure of the system? Why is phase separation unable to occur in CLCE
containing only EDDET?
Our response:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. In the crosslinked network, the self-
assembly of LC mesogens is restricted. For example, it cannot easily undergo temperature-
dependent phase transitions (crystal-smectic-nematic-isotropic) like small-molecule LCs.
The restriction of chain mobility by the cross-linked network is a factor that must be
considered, which imposes higher requirements for phase transitions in polymers. The rod-
like LC mesogens, the inherent long spacer chains of RM82, and the long spacer chains of
chain extenders all contribute to the formation of the smectic phase. (Soft Matter, 2017, 13,
7537-7547) However, for the chiral nematic system in this work, merely extending the
spacer chains is insufficient due to the presence of the helical structure. This gives rise to
the thiol-terminated side chains determined by the synthesis ratio—a strategy to enhance
chain mobility.
The smectic phase requires both orientational order of LC cores and lamellar arrangement.
The long flexible chains of EDDET facilitate lamellar arrangement, but they only tend to
promote the transition from the already orientationally ordered nematic phase to the
smectic phase. For the chiral nematic phase with a helical structure, the key issue lies in
how to induce the helical molecular arrangement into an orientationally ordered state
(where the directions of molecular long axes are nearly uniform). At this point,
crystallizable ODT segments play a role that EDDET does not possess: the arrangement of
crystalline molecular chains is regular (with consistent directions and similar spacings).
This implies that the rod-like cores of nearby LC molecules acquire the characteristic of
orientational order along with the regular arrangement of crystalline molecular chains,
thereby promoting the formation of the smectic phase.
To clarify the reason why phase separation unable to occur in conventional CLCE, we have
revised the manuscript as follows:
"It is noted that the performance difference between SS-CLCE and conventional CLCE
indicated that the presence of ODT affected the ability to undergo phase separation. ODT
segments not only enabled polymer crystallization themselves but also promoted the
formation of the to-be-discussed smectic phase. This is because the rod-like cores of nearby
LC molecules acquire the characteristic of orientational order along with the regular
arrangement of crystalline molecular chains." (Highlighted in Results, page 9, lines 173-
178)
3) The text mentions C-CLCE. What is the main difference in the network structure between
C-CLCE and SS-CLCE? What is its primary role in the experiment?
Our response:
We thank the reviewer for this valuable question. We apologize for the insufficient
explanation of C-CLCE in this paper. As a control sample, it was insufficiently explained
in the initial manuscript. Herein, we will elaborate on its role in the experiment in detail.
During the standing process prior to photopolymerization, oligomers continuously undergo
self-assembly of linear oligomers; prolonged standing leads to the formation of obvious
crystalline regions, which act as optical and mechanical defects in the film (Figure R5).
Therefore, when investigating the optimal photopolymerization time point, we prepared
such a control sample. The corresponding experimental procedure was as follows: after
prolonged standing (>8 h), high-temperature annealing (68-100-68 °C) was performed to
eliminate defects, followed by photopolymerization. The resulting C-CLCE film
theoretically exhibits a higher chain extension degree but lacks the orientation effect
induced by solvent evaporation. There is no difference in chemical composition. The
structural difference between SS-CLCE and C-CLCE lies in the distribution along the
helical axis: the former tends to be vertical, while the latter is disordered. This determines
the presence or absence of reflected color, while the phase separation phenomenon occurs
collectively due to the existence of linear backbones and side chains. Therefore, the
primary role of the C-CLCE is to indicate that standing prior to polymerization is
unfavorable for the film to exhibit N* phase characteristics. However, both samples show
similar XRD patterns and DSC curves, suggesting the presence of the same phase states
and analogous structures (with different orientation conditions). Given the identical raw
material ratios, this indicates that endowing hardening properties requires sacrificing
structural color performance. The differences in material performance after polymerization
demonstrate the importance of polymerization control.
Figure R5. The appearance of the samples at different durations. (Supplementary Fig. 3)
To clarify, we have included the photographs of oligomers at different durations (Figure

that disappeared upon heating." (Highlighted in Results, page 7, lines 139-146)
"When the self-assembly time was further extended to 8 h or more, the influence of the

defined as the controlled CLCE (C-CLCE), which was induced into a vertical alignment
mode due to the absence of orientation effect induced by evaporation." (Highlighted in
Results, page 8, lines 158-164)

Our response:
We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful suggestion. Unfortunately, the SS-CLCE in this
work did not achieve actuating performance, as it did not undergo the stretching orientation

the extension of aging time, the toughness will be further improved (Figure R12).
Figure R12. (a) The increase in material modulus leads to a greater absorption of energy
during deformation. (b) The time-dependent increase of deformation energy. (Figs. 2e and
4c)
To supplement, we note that Kim et al. (Small 2025, 21, 2406493) reported that the
introduction of crystallizable segments into liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs) exerts a
strengthening effect on the materials. As stated in the abstract: "The specially designed
photochemical muscles can undergo about 60% tensile stroke and provide 15 kJ m⁻³ of
work capacity in response to light, thus providing about three times and two times higher
performance, respectively, than previous azobenzene actuators." This excellent work
enhanced the work capacity by improving the modulus and achieved actuation through the
photoresponsiveness of azobenzene rather than the thermally driven actuation related to
the mesogenic orientation of LCEs, thereby avoiding the impact of high temperatures on

5) In Fig. 6c, why does the CLCE film appear white under natural light but show bright
red under R-CP light? It is expected to see red color under natural light as well.
Our response:
We thank the reviewer for this valuable question. It is noted that the visually observed
white actually contains a faint orange-red color, which failed to be captured due to the
masking effect of the white color. Theoretically, right-handed CLCEs selectively reflect
right-handed circularly polarized light of specific wavelengths. In this study, the helical
structures self-assembled by linear oligomers induced via the solvent evaporation method
are arranged along the vertical direction, forming a multi-domain structure. The relatively
weak orientation ability of solvent evaporation results in a wide distribution of helical
directions and pitches of the oligomers, which weakens the circular dichroism
characteristics. Meanwhile, the difference in refractive index for light among different
microdomains leads to intense light scattering, exhibiting non-selective unpolarized light.
Considering comprehensively, the white color under natural light is the combined
result of unpolarized light scattering and broad-peak reflection of right-handed
circularly polarized light. When a right-handed circular polarizer is employed, only the
right-handed polarized light is retained. The central wavelength of the right-handed light
lies in 630 nm, showing an obvious orange-red color) (Figure R13).
Figure R13. Reflection spectrum of SS-CLCE in the phase-separated and unstretched state.
It can be observed that the central wavelength of N* phase reflection is at 630 nm, while
the reflection exhibits a broad peak and a high baseline caused by scattering spanning the
entire visible light region, leading to a white appearance.

page 16, lines 301-304)
"Due to the polydomain and phase-separated nature of the film, its non-selective left-

11) Hybrid Temperature–Time Protocols
Since both temperature and time strongly influence aging, could hybrid or sequential protocols
(e.g., rapid initiation at higher temperature followed by stabilization at lower temperature)
yield.
Our response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this thoughtful suggestion. Our work have shown that
spontaneous phase separation leads to a toughening and strengthening process over time,
while temperature, as a key factor affecting chain mobility, influences the rate of
strengthening. The choice between the two will determine efficiency and rigidity. Earlier,
we also conducted corresponding studies on the influence of thickness, uniformity, and the
possibility of gradient control. These verify that the hardening phenomenon is broadly
applicable. Hybrid control of temperature and time is certainly feasible. We can infer that
if the just-heated films are sequentially aged at higher and lower temperatures for a certain
duration, according to the universal properties of polymer crystallization, the closer the
temperature is to the crystal melting point (below the melting point), the more perfect the
formed crystals will be, and the higher the melting point will be; conversely, a temperature
far from the melting point will result in crystal defects and a lower melting point. This is
the reason why the melting point of polymers is generally referred to as the melting range,
indicating the broad peak form of the melting peak. Therefore, we can anticipate that hybrid
temperature-time control will lead to a wider melting range of the polymer, and the
crystallization properties will also affect the phase transition of the smectic sequence,
resulting in the broadening of the DSC curve. This is unfavorable for selecting appropriate
aging temperatures or heating temperatures in this work. And our work focuses on material
hardening and the resulting memory effect, and hybrid control would complicate this
strategy. Thus, while we agree that the reviewers' suggestions will endow the material
with richer phase transition characteristics and potential significance, the
introduction of more comparative samples is not conducive to elaborating the
viewpoints of this paper, after all, the best way to age is still to maintain a constant
temperature.

14) Interpretation of Stress–Strain Data
Since Figures 4a and 4b show clear spatial heterogeneity in color and reflectance, it is
important to clarify which region (center, edge, etc.) the reported stress–strain curves
represent.
Our response:
We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. We clarify that the stress-strain curves
do not correspond to a specific region but reflect the overall performance of the tested films.
Given the more pronounced spatial heterogeneity of the aged film, we use it as an example
for explanation, correlating the stress-strain curves with the actual stretching process.
1. Elastic deformation stage (strain < 10%)
The rapid stress increase before the yield point corresponds to the elastic deformation of
the entire film reinforced by microphase separation. Within this stage, both deformation
and color change are minimal.
2. Initial microphase separation destruction stage
When a specific point (stress concentration point) reaches the elastic deformation limit, the
initial microphase separation-reinforced structure is destroyed by mechanical forces. The
damaged microphases can no longer withstand higher stress, resulting in a slowed stress
increase rate or even a negative value. Meanwhile, the polymer chains at this location start
to orient along the direction of the external force, while chains at other positions remain
protected by microphase separation without orientation. This corresponds to significant
deformation and narrowing at the specific location of the film, with the color changing
from white to blue-green, while minimal changes are observed in other regions.
3. Plastic deformation plateau stage
As the degree of polymer chain orientation at the stress concentration point increases, the
stress balances with that at the adjacent microphase-reinforced regions. Further strain leads
to the gradual orientation of non-oriented chains adjacent to the oriented ones. This
corresponds to the plastic deformation plateau with slow stress increase, where the blue-
green, large-deformation region gradually expands, and the white region gradually
decreases until it disappears.
In summary, the stress-strain curves we provided represent the overall mechanical
performance of individual films, which is similar to the tensile properties of commodity
plastics. Although local preferential strain occurs during the process (local necking first
occurs at a specific point), this is also a reflection of the overall performance.
To clarify, we have also revised the manuscript as follows:

focused on the strain range of 0 to 100% (Fig. 4c), although local preferential strain occurs
during the process (local necking first occurs at a specific point), this is also a reflection of
the overall performance." (Highlighted in Results, page 18, lines 350-353)

8987–8995) reported that the introduction of long methylene chains into LCEs exerts a
positive effect on crystallization, and specified the aging condition of 24 h at 20 °C. Kim
et al. (Small 2025, 21 ,2406493) reported that the introduction of crystallizable segments
into LCEs exerts a strengthening effect on the materials, and specified the aging condition
as "samples then stored overnight to be crystallized". Ji et al. (Nature Communications
2024, 15, 9902) incorporated crystallized LCEs into the LCE matrix to form a semi-
interpenetrating network, and the article states the following: "The results indicated that
their crystallization behaviors were observed after 1 day, and the crystallization process
could be mostly completed in 5 days." 
Thanks to the reviewers' suggestions, we have realized the significance of shortening the
aging time. Therefore, we have adopted corresponding measures to minimize the
programming time (including increasing the content of crystallizable segments and
raising the programming temperature). This method is based on the temperature
dependence discovered in our experiments combined with the crystallizable segments
emphasized in previous work (Figure 4f). We chose to use ODT as the sole chain extender
(increased from a ratio of 4:1 to 1:0), and the aging temperature of the prepared SS-CLCE
films was set at 40 °C for the time-dependent tests (Figure R11).

is 1:0). Stress-strain curves for strains ranging from 0 to 100% at different aging times at
40 °C
After adjusting the ratio and aging temperature, we observed a faster aging rate, with the
maximum rate occurring between 2 and 6 hours. At this point, 8 hours can be used as the
programming duration, representing a significant improvement compared to the previous
condition. However, all data in the initial manuscript of this work were obtained from SS-
CLCEs prepared with a molar ratio of ODT:EDDET = 4:1. This ratio can better illustrate
our viewpoint—i.e., the promoting effect of side-chain functionalization rather than merely
the introduction of crystallizable segments. Therefore, we hope to retain the main data in
the main text and present the aforementioned experiments as supplementary information
to provide a method for improving material performance.
To clarify, we have added Figure R11 as Supplementary Fig. 24, we have we have also
revised the manuscript as follows:
"Upon heating, it was also capable of reverting to its original state, thereby enabling the
next usage cycle. It is worth noting that the aforementioned programming time requires
more than 24 hours to achieve better memory effect. By introducing more crystallizable
segments and increasing the aging temperature to accelerate chain rearrangement, the
duration can be further shortened to 8 hours (Supplementary Fig. 24)." (Highlighted in
Results, page 24, lines 462-466)
